<reflection>
After two experiments varying catalyst concentration at high substrate, the fitting results show that M5 is currently the best-fitting mechanism, but many others (M4, M11, M7, M3, M14, M18, M2, M1, etc.) have NLL values within ~1-2 units, indicating they are still plausible. The aim of the second turn was to stress the system with a higher catalyst concentration, which did create some separation (M20 became much worse), but further discrimination is needed. To avoid prematurely focusing on the top few, we need an experiment that probes a different dimension of the kinetic space.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
Thus far, we have varied catalyst concentration while keeping substrate high and product absent. The next most informative perturbation is to introduce product initially, which will test for reversible product inhibition and product-dependent deactivation pathways. Many mechanisms differ in their response to product: simple reversible mechanisms (M1, M2) will show equilibrium inhibition; mechanisms with irreversible product deactivation (M12, M17) may exhibit accelerated loss of activity; and mechanisms without product steps will be less affected. By adding a moderate amount of product (0.2 M) while keeping substrate at 1.0 M and catalyst at the lower level (0.01 M), we create a direct comparison with run_1 (same conditions but zero product). This contrast will reveal whether product merely slows the reaction (reversible inhibition) or causes progressive decay (deactivation). The choice of low catalyst avoids confounding with high-catalyst effects already explored and ensures that product-induced deactivation steps (which may be bimolecular with catalyst or catS) are not overshadowed by other processes. This experiment is broadly informative because it touches on a key feature distinguishing many candidate mechanisms.
</hypothesis>
